title: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
summary_raw: Article URL: https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118320 Points: 116 # Comments: 56
fulltext:
Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.
In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model â Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters â right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.
Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.
Running Large Language Models with MLX
We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.
We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts â and thus parameters â active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).
| Model | Total Parameters | Active Parameters | Native Precision | Evaluation Precision | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | 816B | 42B | BF16 | NVFP4 | 
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 128B | 128B | FP8 | FP8 | 
| Qwen 3.8 | 27B | 27B | BF16 | BF16 | 
Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:
mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1
A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.
Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively.
Inference Performance on a Single Mac Studio
Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2, we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.
Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6Ã faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.
Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6Ã faster tokens/s.
The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra â a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.
While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.
Pipelining Inference Across Two Mac Studio Computers
Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the modelâs inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the modelâs layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.

title: anthropics/claude-plugins-official: Official, Anthropic-managed directory of high quality Claude Code Plugins.
summary_raw: Official, Anthropic-managed directory of high quality Claude Code Plugins. [语言: Python] [今日 +1,552 stars]
fulltext:
A curated directory of high-quality plugins for Claude Code.
⚠️ Important: Make sure you trust a plugin before installing, updating, or using it. Anthropic does not control what MCP servers, files, or other software are included in plugins and cannot verify that they will work as intended or that they won't change. See each plugin's homepage for more information.
- /plugins - Internal plugins developed and maintained by Anthropic
- /external_plugins - Third-party plugins from partners and the community
Plugins can be installed directly from this marketplace via Claude Code's plugin system.
To install, run /plugin install {plugin-name}@claude-plugins-official
or browse for the plugin in /plugin > Discover
Internal plugins are developed by Anthropic team members. See /plugins/example-plugin for a reference implementation.
Third-party partners can submit plugins for inclusion in the marketplace. External plugins must meet quality and security standards for approval. To submit a new plugin, use the plugin directory submission form.
Each plugin follows a standard structure:
plugin-name/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json      # Plugin metadata (required)
├── .mcp.json            # MCP server configuration (optional)
├── commands/            # Slash commands (optional)
├── agents/              # Agent definitions (optional)
├── skills/              # Skill definitions (optional)
└── README.md            # Documentation
The name field in a marketplace entry is an immutable slug. Once a plugin has been published, its name must not change — users have it installed under that slug, and renaming it breaks their install with a plugin-not-found error.
- To change how a plugin is labeled in the UI, set or update displayName instead.
- If a rename is genuinely unavoidable, add an entry to the top-level renames map in .claude-plugin/marketplace.json so existing installs auto-migrate:
"renames": {
  "old-name": "new-name"
}
The Claude Code plugin loader reads this map and transparently rewrites the old slug to the new one on the user's next sync.
When a plugin's source repository ships skills (SKILL.md files) without a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest, the marketplace entry can declare the skills directly using strict: false and an explicit skills array.
{
  "name": "example-bundle",
  "description": "Brief description of the bundled skills.",
  "author": { "name": "Author Name" },
  "category": "development",
  "source": {
    "source": "git-subdir",
    "url": "https://github.com/example-org/sdk.git",
    "path": "packages/agent-skills",
    "ref": "main",
    "sha": "<commit sha>"
  },
  "strict": false,
  "skills": [
    "./skill-a",
    "./skill-b",
    "./skill-c"
  ],
  "homepage": "https://github.com/example-org/sdk"
}
Each path in skills is relative to source.path and points at a directory containing a SKILL.md. Paths can reach deeper than a single level — for example, ["./libA/skill-1", "./libB/skill-2"] exposes a curated subset across multiple library subdirectories. Each skill is registered as <plugin-name>:<skill-name> in Claude Code.
For the underlying schema, see Strict mode in the marketplace documentation.
Please see each linked plugin for the relevant LICENSE file.
For more information on developing Claude Code plugins, see the official documentation.

title: Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD
summary_raw: Article URL: https://calif.io/research/big-fish Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118977 Points: 81 # Comments: 14
fulltext:
Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD
Big fish. Small counter. Root shell.
Contents
Calif frequently publishes our offensive research and work, but we otherwise don't draw much attention to the defensive work we do — assisting open source projects with remediation, patch generation, cryptographic improvements, and internal engineering projects we carry out for our clients.
Earlier this year, we reported some vulnerabilities, often along with suggested patches to OpenBSD. One traced back roughly 37 years to the original BSD sources, where a shared memory attachment counter was defined as a signed 16-bit short. Repeatedly forking a process with shared memory attachment records could push that counter past its maximum value of 32,767, causing it to wrap to a negative value. This integer overflow could lead to a use-after-free via a race condition; combined with a separate out-of-bounds write in the kernel, it allowed local privilege escalation to root. The issues were addressed in errata 026 and 018, respectively.
The exploit
We managed to get local root in OpenBSD with KARL / SMAP / SMEP enabled without the use of an information disclosure vulnerability via the following path:
- Map 127 SysV shared memory segments, unmap them via munmap(), and fork 259 processes to wrap the shared memory attach count to -32,643.
- Perform heap grooming and layout, using metrics from sysctl(KERN_MALLOCSTATS) (such as kb_total and kb_totalfree) to track allocations and determine when new pages are allocated.
- Win the race condition using IPC_RMID in one process while attaching a new size-confused shared memory segment in a helper process.
- Align IP socket allocations and set IP_MULTICAST_TTL to a non-default value of 2 to allocate a persistent 16-byte struct ip_moptions. Its final word packs two 16-bit counters: imo + 12 = imo_num_memberships | imo_max_memberships << 16.
- Trigger the conditional -1 out-of-bounds write to overwrite both the number of memberships and maximum memberships fields.
- close() the socket to traverse the group members, triggering atomic decrements that modify the PTE self-referential mapping twice, switching it from user to supervisor accessible mapping, and achieving kernel code execution by overwriting a predictable kernel pointer.
- Clean up shared memory accounting and restore the overwritten kernel pointer to obtain a root shell.
That's the short of the matter, the longer version is more interesting, including the history of the vulnerability, as a short shm_nattch can be traced back ~37 years ago, in the original BSD sources.
Taking a step back, this vulnerability ended up getting code execution via a write what where primitive, where the write was caused by a TAILQ_REMOVE, the what was our userland memory mapping that was made supervisor mode accessible to bypass SMAP/SMEP, and the where was a predictable kernel pointer location.
Exploit mitigation
While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic. Both the boot-time allocator and the best-fit allocator lack base address randomization. Consequently, early boot allocations consistently land at predictable locations across boots on the same hardware. When these predictable structure allocations contain function pointers, they become ideal targets for exploitation. For instance, the exploit reliably targets the lo0 and enc0 ioctl handlers, overwriting one to gain control flow and using the other to restore the overwritten pointer.
Aside from the aforementioned errata fixes, there's several other approaches that can be taken to either eliminate or reduce the likelihood of those avenues being used again.
Firstly, we can implement safe-unlinking, a technique that checks doubly linked list invariants before performing the unlink memory writes. If the invariants are violated, then a suitable abort() or panic() is called, depending on if user mode or kernel mode, preventing memory corruption from occurring. An example implementation is here. FreeBSD and NetBSD have an implementation of safe-unlinking in their sys/queue.h implementation.
Secondly, we can randomize the self-referential PTE map allocation address so that the targeted atomic decrement locations would not be possible. This is done by using a random byte (.openbsd.randomdata) and selecting a PML4 slot (320 + (random_byte & 127)) at boot time, and installing the recursive entry at that location. The PTE_BASE definition becomes a runtime expression, yielding bases from 0xffffa00000000000 through 0xffffdf8000000000 at 512-GiB intervals. An example implementation is here. In case randomization is not suitable, other options might suffice, such as marking the PTE as read-only, and changing CR0.WP during modification.
Thirdly, the kernel allocator can be made non-deterministic using two approaches; by randomizing the base address where memory allocations occur at boot time, and additionally randomizing the allocation order at run time. The base address randomization is effectively free as the gap it creates can still be used later on; while runtime randomization does incur some overhead during allocation - it may be possible that more in-depth allocator changes could alleviate this impact. Either approach would be sufficient to break the predictable pointer location without additional vulnerabilities, be it software or hardware.
Furthermore, there are existing and upcoming compiler features that can be used to mitigate against entire vulnerabilities, from array bounds sanitizer (a subset of Undefined Behaviour sanitizer) which can eliminate out of bounds fixed size array accesses. title: Desire to Move Permanently to U.S. at New Low
summary_raw: Article URL: https://news.gallup.com/poll/708614/desire-migrate-drops-new-low.aspx Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50120664 Points: 36 # Comments: 11
fulltext:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. remains the most desired destination for people who would like to leave their own countries permanently, but Gallup's latest data show it is less attractive than it once was.
In 2025, 15% of adults worldwide who say they would like to move permanently to another country name the U.S. as their preferred destination, the lowest level recorded in nearly two decades of Gallup research. From 2007 to 2009, 24% of would-be migrants named the U.S. as their top choice, and that figure remained near 20% through 2016. Since 2017, it has been at or below 18%.
The rank order of the countries attracting the most interest from potential migrants has seen little change since Gallup’s first measure. Canada ranks second, as it has for several years, with 9% of potential migrants mentioning the U.S. neighbor. The appeal of these desired destinations did not change in 2025, even as the U.S. became less desirable.
Line charts show trends in the percentage of adults worldwide who would like to move permanently to top destination countries from 2007–2009 to 2025. The United States remains the top destination but declines from 24% to 15%. Canada rises from 7% to 9%. The United Kingdom declines from 7% to 4%. Germany, Australia, Spain, France, Japan, Italy, and Saudi Arabia remain broadly stable around 3% to 5%.
Gallup's latest update on migration desire is based on a question asked almost annually: “Ideally, if you had the opportunity, would you like to move permanently to another country, or would you prefer to continue living in this country?” Those who say they would like to move are then asked to name their preferred destination.
Results for 2025 are based on interviews with over 144,000 adults in 140 countries. The current estimates include data from China for 2023, the last time the question was asked there.
The most recent analysis period coincides with a sharp slowdown in international migration into the U.S., amid changes in immigration policy and declining migration desire in several regions. External data suggest global migration more broadly slowed in 2024 after surging post-pandemic.
Declining Desire to Move to the U.S.
The U.S. became less attractive to adults in several regions in 2025, with statistically significant declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia.
Latin America accounts for seven of the 16 countries worldwide where the percentage naming the U.S. as a preferred destination fell by at least 10 points. In the region, the percentage fell from 33% in 2024 to 28% in 2025.
Other Latin American countries that saw double-digit declines include U.S. neighbor Mexico, where the latest 21% who want to move to the U.S. matches the previous low set in 2017 and 2018. In Honduras, desire to migrate to the U.S. dropped 35 percentage points, from 71% to 36%, the largest decline in any country in 2025.
Despite the falling numbers, the U.S. remains by far the most desired destination in Latin America and the Caribbean and in sub-Saharan Africa. The picture varies more in other regions.
In Southeast Asia, Japan leads at 23%, compared with 12% for the U.S. In the Middle East and North Africa, Germany attracts 13% and Saudi Arabia 12% of potential migrants, with the U.S. at 9%. In South Asia, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. are roughly tied, each cited by 7%. Within the European Union, Spain, at 11%, and Switzerland, at 8%, rank ahead of the U.S., at 6%.
Global Desire to Migrate Falls, Shifts
Beyond where people want to go, the data also show a shift in how many want to move at all.
Overall, global desire to migrate declined in 2025 to its lowest level in a decade, driven by sharp drops in regions that have long had the highest migration aspirations, including Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa. After holding at a record-high 16% between 2021 and 2024, global desire dipped in 2025 for the first time in years, falling one point to 15%, a level not seen since 2018.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, 25% of adults say they would like to move permanently to another country, the lowest level in a decade. The decline is particularly notable in this region, where migration desire has fallen steadily after peaking at 34% in 2021-2022.
Multiple countries across the region recorded double-digit declines between 2024 and 2025. In Honduras and El Salvador, the percentage of adults wanting to leave fell sharply last year, from levels above 50% in several prior years to 35% and 25%, respectively.
In sub-Saharan Africa, where migration desire remains the highest globally, 33% say they would like to move permanently, also a decade low. As recently as 2023, that figure stood at 37%, ticking upward from 36% in 2021-2022.
In regions that are typically on the receiving end of migrants, the picture is different. Migration desire in the United States and Canada (20%) and the European Union (21%) remains near record highs.
In the U.S., notably, the heightened desire to move abroad is concentrated among women younger than 45. In 2025, 40% of U.S. women aged 15 to 44 say they would move permanently to another country if they had the opportunity, up from 10% in 2014. The trend first rose sharply in 2016 and continued across multiple years, suggesting a broader shift in outlook rather than a short-term political effect.
Bottom Line
It is important to note that desire to migrate is not the same as intent to move. Not everyone who wants to move can or will do so. The 2025 data show that fewer people worldwide are imagining their futures elsewhere, and the U.S., long the world’s most desired destination, is attracting less of that interest than at any point in nearly two decades.
For years, the dominant story in global migration data was a rising desire to move across nearly every region. The 2025 data suggest that pattern is shifting. The declines are widespread and concentrated in the regions that have historically driven global migration.

title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
summary_raw: Article URL: https://jakearchibald.com/2026/jpeg-xl-vs-avif/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50120224 Points: 27 # Comments: 6
fulltext:
JPEG XL vs AVIF for web use-cases
JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.
Conclusions
I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:
For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15â25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6â20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.
The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel, a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl, except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.
For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30â90% larger at default effort settings, and 20â70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.
For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31â44% larger at default effort settings, and 61â70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2â3x the size of AVIF's. See the data.
AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.
AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2â3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.
Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.
AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.
Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data.
Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data.
AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself.
For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples.
JPEG XL can make existing JPEGs 9â20% smaller, without further loss. It's also as fast or faster to decode, except for small images. See the data.
For lossless, JPEG XL is the clear winner. Lossless WebP is 9â17% larger for photos, and lossless AVIF is 30â120% larger. But lossless images are almost never what you want on the web. If you do use them on the web (like I do on this page), watch out for jixel's higher efforts - it often produces files that are too slow to decode. See the data.
Animated image formats continue to be a dumb idea. Please don't use them. Learn more, if you must.
For web use-cases, I'd currently default to AVIF 4:4:4, with the highest effort level I can be bothered with. If I felt AVIF was producing an unusually large file, I'd take a look at JPEG XL via jixel, and see if it did better.
Both AVIF and JPEG XL (via jixel) have seen massive improvements recently, so it's possible that this recommendation could change in future. There's been a lot of misinformation around this stuff, and your AI will happily deliver that misinformation to you. Instead, test things with your own images.
AVIF folks suggest that JPEG XL is technically limited compared to AVIF. That might be true, but in this article I'm focusing on results with today's implementations.
Methodology
I 'created' a benchmarking script, that encodes images using various codecs at various settings, and records various details.
I'm using the latest released versions of the image codecs, which at time of writing is:
- avifenc 1.4.2
- libjxl 0.12.0 (using its cjxl encoder)
- jixel 0.4.2 (git f487299), a second JPEG XL encoder
- cwebp 1.6.0 (lossless WebP is used later in the article)

Polymarket, the prediction market platform, is paying social media users to quote-retweet content from its branded esports accounts. The program includes over 800 participants, according to posts by a Polymarket representative in an internal Discord, and offers rates ranging from $10 to several hundred per post, paid in crypto.
Paying social media users to engage with content is not illegal, and the Polymarket program has robust guidelines around disclosure and the kinds of quote retweets the company is looking for. But the slight “Paid partnership” tag on X — a common sight on the app, and the only public indication that there’s money changing hands — belies the scale and sophistication of Polymarket’s esports operation, which has more than doubled in size since August. And all the while, in the Discord, Polymarket representatives have repeatedly reminded participants in the program to write posts in a way that should appear “organic,” in what one expert said was an effort to ingratiate the prediction market with esports fans and casual observers.
“Literally this needs to look organic and if your X profile looks like Polymarket billboard that looks absoutely [sic] awful,” wrote one Polymarket rep in the Discord.
Polymarket offers two products: Polymarket Global, which is inaccessible to bettors in the United States, and Polymarket US, which is subject to U.S. regulations. In esports — a growing market for the company — Polymarket offers lines around the outcomes of major events and matches, player statistics, as well as novelty bets, including some relating to the teams that players might transfer to in the off-season.1
The prediction market company’s esports outreach is something of an open secret in the esports world — with an emphasis on “open.” Some social media users have expressed dismay over the increasing prevalence of gambling and betting-adjacent companies in the esports scene, having previously been burnt by “here today, gone tomorrow” attention from deep-pocketed crypto companies and venture capital firms. But while elements of the paid marketing program have previously been reported, little concrete information has been revealed until now about the logistical apparatus behind it, the costs involved, and the Discord server from which the program is run — even as the payments by Polymarket to creators have inspired speculation and debate among esports fans.
Emails to Polymarket’s official press line seeking comment, as well as direct messages to numerous Polymarket representatives from the Discord seeking interviews, went unanswered.
A list of participants in the Discord includes prominent esports commentators, current and former professional players, team coaches and managers, media entrepreneurs and content creators, PR professionals, amateur roster reporters, employees of esports tournament organizers, and various social media gadflies.
When figures like that quote-retweet posts like the one embedded below with a sentence or two of commentary, they may be receiving tens or even hundreds of dollars in compensation.
Still, many of the posters paid to quote-retweet Polymarket’s content are virtual unknowns, with low four-figure follower counts on X.
Prospective participants in the marketing program are typically contacted via social media or email. If they show interest in continuing the conversation, they’re brought into a Polymarket Discord server. In that server, dedicated channels for individual esport titles ping users about the tweets they should quote-retweet — which generally focus on some ongoing event or storyline, and the corresponding market on which users can bet, which is linked to in the post.
“New tweet is up: Like + QRT. Replies appreciated,” reads a typical message, which includes a link to the tweet. “Text-only quote from your own account. Counts for the next 24 hours only.” These messages used to also include the phrase “+ Paid Partnership tag,” urging users to disclose their participation in the program. That text has not appeared on the Discord prompts since late August, for reasons that were not immediately clear.
Users are concurrently onboarded to a proprietary tool called PolyTrack, a dashboard into which they can input their tax information, crypto wallet address, and eventually, the quote-retweets for which they will be paid. The platform tracks monthly and lifetime earnings, and offers guidance about the kinds of posts that meet the program’s criteria.
While this report is exclusively focused on Polymarket’s promotional efforts on X, PolyTrack also includes the option to input video and streaming platforms.

A story of wifi secrets, UART lockdowns and a damaged flash memory chip
Dear Fellowlship, just as we announced in our previous post, our beloved God Debugger has seen fit to cast his divine light -laden with opcodes- upon his humble servant, and we have a new homily here in our temple. Please, take a seat and listen to the story of how one of our owls, along with his brother-in-law, moved on to dissect the next component of the Eufy ecosystem: the Eufy HomeBase 2.
Prayers at the foot of the Altar a.k.a. disclaimer
We focused our analysis in Eufy Homebase2 instead of Homebase3 because, as we explained in From your doorbell to your home network it’s the version that I found deployed in my city, and also was the easiest to buy. The firmware version we analyze here is 3.4.2.2h (2026-06-05 18:45:48)
This is the first time I touched something related to “hardware”. I always did vuln hunting on firmwares that I could download from internet, so please forgive the sins I commited
IMPORTANT!!! You must read first the previous article before you continue reading this one.
Table of contents
Just as with the previous article, we will be covering a variety of topics here; consequently, some members of this fellowlship may have no interest in certain sections and might wish to skip straight to whatever appeals to them most. That is why we present this blessed offering: a table of contents.
- 0x00 Firmware extraction. Description of how the firmware was extracted (and how we damaged part of the flash memory).
- 0x01 Identifying the Wifi credential generation algorithm. Reverse Engineering the algorithm used to generate the Wifi credential for OCEAN_XXXXXX management wifi.
- 0x02 Rubber-hose treatment to the UART lockdown. Reflashing a backdoored U-Boot image to get a shell via UART.
- 0x03 Filesystem gardening for debugging purposes. Recovery image is limited so some filesystem quirks are needed in order to run the main binary.
- 0x04 Final Words. I share the lack of enthusiasm for writing articles in the age of AI.
0x00 Firmware extraction
In the previous chapter of this saga, I mentioned that we were only able to extract the doorbell’s firmware because the Homebase’s flash memory was soldered directly to the board and did not expose any pins to which we could attach test hooks to dump the firmware. Initially we did not want to desolder it (although in the end we had to as I will explain later) so I had to wait to acquire additional hardware. Craig S. Blackie pointed me to spring clips that would suit the size needed for the Winbond 25Q256JWEQ (WSON8 8.6mm). Once the clip arrived I created the most makeshift setup imaginable, using rubber bands to secure the clip while I proceeded to take readings using the Raspberry Pi’s SPI0 interface, just as we did with the doorbell.
I performed three reads and the three had different checksums, which usually is a indicator of something being wrong. After inspecting the dumps, I quickly realized they were garbage and completely useless. Unlike with the doorbell, in this case, the power supplied for the read operation also activated other components on the board that interacted with the memory; therefore, to extract the firmware, we had to desolder the chip and read it off-board.
My brother-in-law (Óscar Lestón) was the brave soul that desoldered the flash memory (I was too scared to even try it):
Although the memory module looked terrible once removed, it was barely damaged…
And finally we replicated the same setup using the Raspberry Pi SPI 0 to dump the firmware. This time the three dumps had the same checksum and contained “interesting data”. The only problem was… a block of 64kbs was erased / could not be read, highly probable because we damaged it when extracting the chip.
Most of the firmware could be extracted using Binwalk.

title: What on Earth Is Dekton?
summary_raw: Article URL: https://www.worksinprogress.news/p/porcelain Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118828 Points: 63 # Comments: 19
fulltext:
This is our fifth article from Issue 26, which arrived with print subscribers last week. In it, Charles C Mann explains how he learned to love porcelain.
I am aware that I am a bit of a kitchen equipment nerd, okay? So maybe you don’t have to roll your eyes theatrically like my cousins did when I tell you my wife and I got a swanky induction cooktop that was, well, kind of pricey for a middle-class couple? And maybe you can imagine my irritation when it turned out that the swanky induction cooktop – did I mention it was pricey? – did not include the necessary smooth cooking surface above the induction burners, and that you had to buy the cooking surface separately from a separate company, a fact not exactly advertised on the website, and that the surface could not be tempered glass, which is what I had thought was on top of induction ranges, a sheet of which costs maybe $30 per square foot, but a special, newly created material called Dekton that cost five times as much. ‘What on earth is Dekton?’ I asked the heavens, or at least my wife.
My question turned out to have two answers. The first is that Dekton is an artificial material invented by the Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 that is amazingly heat-, pressure-, scratch-, shatter-, and stain-resistant – a high-tech substance that would have been almost impossible to fashion even thirty years ago. The other answer, equally true, is that Dekton is basically porcelain.
Paradoxically, porcelain is both one of humankind’s oldest high technologies and one of its newest. The earliest proto-porcelain was created more than three thousand years ago, and was, for the time, an astonishing technical feat, as unprecedented as the roughly concurrent development of iron metallurgy. Iron technology had its second flowering in the mid-nineteenth century, when the invention of the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin refining processes allowed manufacturers to produce cheap, high-quality steel. Porcelain is having its resurgence today – indeed, high-tech ceramics are key elements in the ongoing upsurge in materials science, the study of the relationship between a substance’s structure and its physical properties.
Much attention is rightfully focused now on the rise of the digital world and the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence. But that attention sometimes obscures the ongoing, equally important transformation of our physical world, the built environment, by materials science. Unleashing a cataract of innovation so ubiquitous as to be almost invisible, materials science has literally changed the walls around us. Porcelain is a reminder that the drive to create new types of matter has long played a powerful role in human history.
Kaolin
The initial steps toward porcelain occurred when potters in northern China started to tinker with an unusual clay, chalk colored and fine grained, called kaolin. Kaolin was known for its color, useful in paints, coatings, and fillers. Potters learned that subjecting this soft, white, unremarkable-looking mud to extreme temperatures produced startling effects.
Ordinary clay looks like amorphous glop but actually is composed of huge numbers of microscopic crystals. The crystals have an unusual structure: flat plates stacked atop each other like playing cards in a deck, loosely held together by hydroxyl groups (hydrogen and oxygen bound together, or -OH, in chemists’ terms). When clay is cooked in a kiln, the hydroxyl groups vibrate and break free, causing the plates to fall apart and reform into long, needle-shaped crystals that lock together into a sturdy structure. Meanwhile, the free hydroxyls merge, becoming water molecules that steam away in the hot kiln, leaving behind oxygen in the new crystals.
Kaolin clay is abundant in kaolinite, a mineral made of aluminum, silicon, oxygen, and hydrogen – Al2Si2O5(OH)4, with the parentheses meaning that each molecule has four hydroxyl groups. When heated in a kiln, kaolinite also loses its hydroxyls and reorganizes itself into a three-dimensional web of needle-like crystals. But when the temperature rises to about 1,200 degrees centigrade, well above the typical level for earthenware pottery, kaolin does something else. The silicon and oxygen break free, forming silica, which forms a thick liquid glass, filling all the spaces around and inside the web of needles, creating a dense, continuous, translucent matrix – porcelain.
In China, like everywhere else, ceramics had been a foundational industry for millennia. Clay was a primary part of construction (bricks, adobe, wattle-and-daub), cooking (pots, tableware), art (paints as well as sculpture), and even communication – clay tablets were the first surfaces used for writing. But porcelain was a giant leap, a concatenation of multiple innovations.
Ordinary kilns couldn’t reach the temperatures required to fire porcelain, partly because their exhaust vents, located on the ‘roof’, let out the hot air almost as fast as it was created, cooling the kiln. (This is a problem for conventional home fireplaces, which are fun to look at in use but wildly inefficient as a means of heating.) Chinese potters designed downdrafts, which forced the hot air to escape through floor vents, trapping the heat around the pottery. Alarmingly, ordinary kilns would shatter or even melt at such high temperatures. Chinese potters invented new types of heat-resistant brick. And so on.
Alltinktur
When Europeans first saw East Asian porcelain, probably in the thirteenth century, they were astounded. Harder, stronger, finer, smoother, and more lustrous than any other pottery, it became an obsessive object of desire, ‘white gold’ for the Continent’s wealthy and powerful. Enormous sets of gleaming white china became symbols of luxury – the private jets and invite-only clubs of the Renaissance era.
Unhappy about the high prices charged by the merchants who imported porcelain from Asia, European elites spent lavishly on efforts to make their own porcelain – and fail

title: How to Formalize All of Mathematics
summary_raw: Article URL: https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/10/16/how-to-formalize-all-of-mathematics/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118512 Points: 46 # Comments: 42
fulltext:
(This is a guest post, written by Jeremy Avigad, Kevin Buzzard, Johan Commelin, Rémy Degenne, Kim Morrison, Oliver Nash and Adam Topaz.)
Mathematicians’ reactions to last week’s big OpenAI release range from excitement to frustration, but one thing is clear: AI has become remarkably good at proving theorems, both formally and informally. The successes in the formal realm have led AI enthusiasts to declare that now is the time to formalize all of mathematics as a legacy for future generations.
We are sympathetic to this proposal. We recognize the power of new technologies for mathematical reasoning and appreciate what they can contribute to the subject we know and love. We are generally optimistic about the role AI can play, but we are deeply concerned by some recent calls to formalize everything as quickly as possible. If done well, a large-scale, coordinated formalization effort could enormously expand mathematical exploration and discovery. Done poorly, it will be, at best, a waste of resources; more likely, it will do lasting damage.
We prefer to see formalization done well. This post therefore clarifies our concerns, describes some of our experiences with AI and formalization, and offers a positive vision of how we can all work toward a world in which all, or almost all, mathematical definitions, theorems, and proofs are equipped with a formal representation, and in which these artifacts help mathematics flourish.
Just as the role of AI in mathematics is a fraught subject these days, so too is its role in formalization. The range of attitudes among expert formalizers toward AI is as wide as the range of attitudes among mathematicians more broadly. We are aware that some of our closest friends and colleagues, whose opinions we value and respect highly, stand strongly opposed to large-scale formalization using AI. Nothing we say here should be taken as representative of the views of any of the organizations or communities with which we are associated.
The concerns
Let’s start with the observation that a formal artifact is not worth much if nobody uses it. When Math, Inc. tried to hijack a project to formalize Maryna Viazovska’s higher-dimensional sphere-packing results last February, it impressively demonstrated what the technology could do, but beyond that, it contributed nothing to mathematics. The original project team kept preparing a quality formalization of the 8-dimensional result and soon discovered that cleaning up the AI-generated code was more trouble than it was worth; it turned out it was better to throw the code away and do it right, still with ample help from AI.
When Anthropic announced that Claude had formally verified Fermat’s Last Theorem with 13 million lines of code written over 11 days, Kevin Buzzard cheerfully lauded the result while also declaring he had no intention of ending his ongoing formalization of a more modern proof. Once again, although the accomplishment is impressive, this piece of AI-generated code probably has little ongoing value.
What is going on here? The theorems were not seriously in doubt, so the value of the formal artifacts lies solely in what we get beyond mere correctness. We want to formalize everything because we want to use the formalizations to do more mathematics, and to do it better than we could have done without them. We want to think about possible generalizations, explore connections between different branches of mathematics, and consider unexpected applications. We want to refactor and improve our knowledge: part of the joy of manual formalization comes from realizing that we can adjust our concepts to make them more elegant, more efficient, and better suited to our purposes. Knowledge isn’t worth having until it contributes to our understanding; the value of a formalization comes from our ability to use and interact with the data.
When OpenAI announced solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations that blow up in finite time, the natural-language proof was accompanied by a Lean formalization. In contrast to the previous examples, the correctness signal played a key role here: there seems to be little doubt now that the solution is correct, even though the natural-language proof is mostly incomprehensible. OpenAI nonetheless drew the mathematics community’s anger over concerns about how it obtained the result, provenance and credit for ideas, and worries that focusing on correctness alone discouraged the exploration and understanding the Millenium prize was meant to foster. So, even here, the unadorned formal artifact is a mixed blessing. OpenAI’s later dump contains astonishing and important mathematics, and at the same time shows a remarkable disregard for readers and for building understanding (some results have been retracted, many of the informal/formal pairs diverge in subtle or significant ways, and most of the informal writeups are impenetrable).
This explains our concern. If spending millions of dollars to formalize mathematics results in libraries nobody uses, it will be a terrible waste of resources. Worse, the project could disincentivize good research and productive use of AI, disrupt the social norms and practices research depends on, and set the field back decades. A grand failure will make it hard, or even impossible, to recover later. A lousy formalization of existing results is worse than no formalization at all.
The positives
Some of the results from the big labs have been done well: OpenAI’s unit distance conjecture work, and Anthropic’s work on the density of Riemann zeta zeroes stand out. They demonstrated impressive new capabilities, contributed to understanding, and the community subsequently built on their work. These are examples of how the labs can contribute positively and we invite further constructive partnerships between the research community and the labs.
Good formal libraries will enable the positive vision we have for the future of mathematical research. Humans, AIs, and the Lean language work in c

fulltext:
RFC8950: Announce IPv4 with an IPv6 next-hop
For the last few days I have been playing with RFC8950 setup, which allows routing of IPv4 on top of IPv6. While logically it’s quite simple, it has a very powerful application towards making “IPv4 an optional” feature riding on top of an IPv6 network (but without any tunnels!)
Some of the interesting use cases:
- A large network can run IPv6 only everywhere on its core and leave IPv4 only on edge devices. This can work without customers doing any tweaking at their end. They still do things the old way but Backbone can run IPv6 only at its core.
- An IP transit backbone can run IPv6 only while exchanging IPv4 routes with its customers/peers/upstream over IPv6 sessions. So IPv4 as a “feature” stays but the network in itself is IPv6 only without the overhead of IPv4 interface config, BGP session config, firewall config, etc.
- An IXP can offer services without IPv4 essentually by using a (unique) IPv6 at the IX LAN & running route server to exchange both IPv4 & IPv6 routes over the IPv6 only session.
Thus what 464XLAT did to the mobile networks - this has the potential to do that for the backbone networks.
How does it work?
Multi-protocol BGP (MP-BGP) supports announcement of IPv4 routes over IPv6 sessions with IPv4 next-hops and IPv6 routes over IPv4 sessions with IPv6 next-hops. RFC8950 extends this feature for IPv4 to have IPv6 next-hops. So for IPv4 address, next hop is IPv6, IPv6 reach works via usual NDP and IPv4 rides on ethernet frames to the same MAC as discovered by the NDP. Technically RFC8950 only impacts control plane decisions by using IPv6 as the control plane but keeps the data plane as it is. IPv4 stays IPv4 & goes as IPv4 over the wire unlike say some tunnel or 464xLAT etc.
Hardware support
As of now it’s quite widely supported by a lot of routing platforms like Juniper JunOS, Cisco IOS XR, Nokia SR OS, Mikrotik, Huawei, BIRD, FRR etc. So, it is very likely supported if you are running a recent version of the OS.
Demo lab
Here’s a fun lab with two customer routers: C1 & C2 connected via provider routers R1-R2-R3 in Container Lab. All routers here are running open source FRR.
- C1 is IPv6 only on the WAN side facing R1. It originates 10.0.0.0/24 to R1 over an IPv6 session.
- R1 & R2 are IPv6 only with no IPv4 anywhere on their interfaces (but carry IPv4 routes in their table)
- R3 has IPv6 with R2 but just IPv4 only with C2. So C2 is like a typical enterprise user who lacks IPv6 deployment and still wants IPv4 only to work.
- R3 has 100.64.0.0/24 and originates it in the IPv4 table (to IPv6 adjacency - R2)
- C2 sits on 100.64.0.2/30 given by R3 and communicate in IPv4 only.
- C1 and C2 can reach each other over this network with parts being IPv6 only without any tunnel.

title: I Love Software Rendering
summary_raw: Article URL: https://www.jamesfmackenzie.com/2026/10/13/i-love-software-rendering/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50117746 Points: 198 # Comments: 144
fulltext:
I love software rendering. The best DOS experience I’ve had in a long while was Quake in its software renderer at 800×600, running at a locked 60fps on my Dell OptiPlex 380. It’s one of the best-looking things I’ve seen a DOS game do.
That’s not how most people remember those games looking. In the 90s you either ran them in software at a low resolution, or you bought a 3D card and played the accelerated version. Today there’s a third option: run the software renderer on a machine fast enough to push it at resolutions nobody could use back then.
What software rendering is
In a software-rendered game, the CPU draws every pixel. There’s no 3D card involved: the game works out each frame in its own code and writes it straight to video memory. Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood and the original Quake all work this way.
When 3D cards arrived, many games got accelerated versions. GLQuake came after Quake, and Blood and Tomb Raider got 3dfx modes. Those versions hand the drawing to the graphics card, and they look different.
Why I like the look
It’s sharp. Software renderers generally sample textures pixel by pixel, so every texel stays a crisp square. Early 3D cards smoothed textures with bilinear filtering, which looked impressive in 1997 but turns everything soft and blurry to my eye now.
It’s gritty. Most of these games ran in 256 colours, with lighting done through lookup tables into that palette. Shadows fall off in visible steps rather than smooth gradients. Technically that’s colour banding, a limitation. In practice it gives the games a rough, grimy texture that I really like, and that hardware rendering smooths away.
It’s how the games were built. Quake was released with its software renderer, and GLQuake followed. Doom and the Build engine games were designed around their software renderers from the start.
It isn’t always the better option. When I got a Voodoo 2 running in a modern PC, Blood ran fast in its 3dfx mode, but the VESA software modes were the better-looking option. Tomb Raider went the other way: its underwater sections look noticeably better accelerated than in the DOS software renderer. So it’s a preference, not a rule. But for most of the games I care about, I’d pick the software renderer.
It’s not just nostalgia, either. Ion Fury, a Build engine game from 2019, still ships with a software renderer.
The catch: it needs a fast PC
Software rendering scales with the CPU. Every extra pixel is work for the processor, so the high VESA resolutions that many late DOS games offered were well beyond the hardware of the day.
Modern hardware can power through most of it. On the OptiPlex 380, Quake at 800×600 holds a locked 60fps. But the heaviest games still push even very fast machines. In his video on the Portwell RUBY-9719, Rasteri shows Build engine games needing far more power at high resolutions, to the point where even a 3.3GHz quad-core Xeon “isn’t quite enough to run Shadow Warrior at full 1600 by 1200”.
So if you want to see these games at their best, you want the fastest machine you can get that still runs them.
Why it needs native DOS
There are other ways to get software rendering on a modern PC. Source ports of Doom and Quake run software renderers on Windows, and Ion Fury runs on Windows natively. They’re great.
What I’m after is the original DOS versions running as they were released, on real hardware. DOSBox is the obvious alternative, but some DOS titles struggle in DOSBox, while on real hardware they behave exactly as intended.
That leaves one more problem: sound. A fast machine running native DOS needs a sound card the games can talk to, and modern PCs don’t have one. That’s a story of its own.
Games worth trying
- Quake, in software at 800×600 or higher
- Duke Nukem 3D and Blood, the Build engine games, at high VESA resolutions
- Screamer

title: Bark: The Toll-Free BBS for 90s Teens
summary_raw: Article URL: https://blog.bityard.net/articles/2026/October/bark-the-toll-free-bbs-for-90s-teens Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50117504 Points: 30 # Comments: 9
fulltext:
Topics: Retrocomputing
The other day I was thinking about the first communities I found online and, perhaps tangentially, to what degree they influenced the amount of therapy I now require to function normally as an adult. Our family's second computer came from Sam's Club. It was a 386DX with Windows 3.0 but my inner nerd would have nothing to do with cheerful bit-mapped color schemes, preferring instead to exit to MS-DOS and do all necessary computing and gaming from a command prompt and text-based GUIs. Hardware-wise, it looked and felt cheap. The machine was less reliable than the cardboard box it came in. It was a Packard Bell and if you were to read this paragraph to anyone who was into computers in the 1990's, they will hear that name and then simply close their eyes and nod quietly in sympathetic understanding.
(Nostalgic Modem Noises)
Most importantly, it came with a dial-up modem. My mom's series of reactions when I told her I had plugged our new computer into the telephone line were as follows:
- "Huh, you can do that?"
- "But why would you do that?"
- "WHAT HAVE YOU DONE AND HOW MUCH DO WE OWE?!"
Now in my defense, as a semi-rebellious teenager eager to experience literally anything outside languid rural Midwest life, I often leaned hard into the practice of begging forgiveness in lieu of asking permission. Sometimes I even got away with it.
To give a better idea of the timeline and circumstances, the Internet as we know today it only kind of existed in the early 90's. There was email, there were message boards, file exchange programs, remote login to other systems, real-time chat (IRC) and so on. The web was new and promising and free of ads but not at all the main attraction just yet. And unless you lived in a city or attended a university with a well-funded technology department, the Internet was probably not yet accessible to you. Or for the purposes of this article, me.
But bulletin board systems (BBSes) had been around since at least the early 80's. Maybe earlier, I'm not sure. These were computers connected to phone lines. When you called a number with your computer, the other computer answered, and you could interact with whatever software the sysop (system operator) had set up. Usually these contained at least public and private message boards, but many also had places where you could download and upload files, chat in real time with others (if the BBS had multiple lines), or play games.
How I came upon the early essentials necessary to connect our computer to other computers is a complete mystery to me at this point. I didn't know anyone else with a modem and my school's computer situation was about a decade behind: "computer" classes were really typing classes taught by a cartoon cat named PAWS on Apple IIs. Back at home, at a bare minimum, I would have needed a terminal program to dial up and interact with another computer. So did I have one already or did I grab one off a shareware floppy that came in some magazine? Where did I even find the number of the first BBS (bulletin-board system) to call?
What happened next is easier to remember. I racked up quite the collection of informative text files from that first handful of BBSes I found, which generally included programming guides, hacking e-zines (Phrack!), some anarchy-type content, and rather entertaining but unhinged conspiracy theories. And of course, where to find more BBSes. I also clearly remember downloading as much software as I could get my hands on. Plenty of development tools, different modem terminal programs, and scads of DOS utilities. I learned a lot in a very short amount of time about BBS software, doors, Kermit, X/Y/Zmodem and ZIP files. It took about two hours to download enough data to fill up a 1.44MB floppy disk over a 2400 baud modem. (Eventually I managed to con my mom into buying a 14.4kbps modem a little bit later. I still have no idea how. Maybe because we had a free trial of Prodigy and that needed a faster modem to draw all the fancy vector graphics?)
But that all came to a swift end when my mom got the phone bill at the end of the month. In those days, local calls were free, long distance calls cost money. You paid by the minute and it was not especially cheap. The problem was, we lived in a town so small you could just about trip over it on your way to somewhere interesting, so everything outside a 1.5-mile radius was long distance. I never heard what the monetary damage was, but she did state in no uncertain terms that it would not be allowed to happen again.
1-800-YOU-NERD
(Don't actually call this, I don't know where it goes.)
One of the files I happened to grab was a list of toll-free BBSes. Or as we'd say back before more toll-free codes were added, "1-800 numbers." I didn't know exactly what I would find at these numbers, but that was a big part of the appeal. The first list I downloaded was TB01-94.TXT by Doug Schneider. Here are some others that I have in my collection from around that time frame:
- TB06-96.TXT - Newer version of "The Best 800 List", also in in the wayback machine. (Click on the ZIP, not the TXT.)
- ECBALAM.TXT - "1-800- BBS'S ACROSS THE US" by Bryan Balam - Date Unknown
- BBSWORK3.TXT - "BBS's That Actually Work!" by Kevin Ardoin - August 1994
- BBSWOR41.TXT - "BBS's That Actually Work!" by Kevin Ardoin - December 1994
- TRANSBBS.TXT - "TRANSPORTATION-RELATED ELECTRONIC BULLETIN BOARD SYSTEMS (BBS)"
I have a very clear memory of trying numbers in some semi-random order, crossing off the ones that never answered and highlighting interesting ones to come back to later. I wrote notes next to some. The crossed-off lines outnumbered the highlighted lines 10-to-1 at least. If I ran into a busy signal, it would sometimes be quite a while before I came back to it. It turned out that these toll-free computer systems came and went faster than people could update and pass around the text files. The vast majority of the numbers I called responded with any of:
- Endles

title: The Folders Programming Language
summary_raw: Article URL: https://danieltemkin.com/esolangs/folders Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50114342 Points: 178 # Comments: 31
fulltext:
The Folders Language
Created 2015 | Updated 2026 | One of Forty-Four Esolangs, by the creator of Rivulet and Velato
Where directories are code and drive space is infinite
About
Folders is a non-textual language, where code is expressed in containment and order alone. The names of the folders are ignored, apart from alphabetical ordering. In other words, they are pure ordered trees.
Inspired by the Whitespace language, Folders is devoted to the idea of dematerialized code. It began with the question What is more empty than a file with no visible text? The empty folder is clutter, an appendage with no purpose. In git, it is ignored entirely (for this reason, it is suggested that Folders programs put .gitignore files in their deepest reaches).
Folders began as a Windows language. In Windows, folders are an even more extreme measure of emptiness: they take up no disk space at all. For proof, create 352,449 folders and get properties on it. In this way, Folders offers not only a dematerialized approach to code but also infinite storage capacity. Keep all your data encoded in folder names and never worry about running out of space again.
For those who use other operating systems, the emulator below gives some of the experience of how Folders manages data and code.
The original implementation can be found on github.
Encoding
Each command folder has at least one child folder. The number of subfolders in the first folder (alphabetically) indicates the type of command; any arguments are indicated in a second folder; some commands require a third folder. Expressions are the same: the number of folders in the first sub-folder determine what kind of expression it is. The full Language Spec is below.
Temporary data is stored as folders; unlike Folders code, it is the name of the folder that stores the data.
Folders FS
The Folders interpreter does not create temp files; anything not held immediately in memory is stored as a set of temp folders. Unlike Folders code, the name of the folder stores the data itself. The prefered I/O of Folders is another set of folders. This means you can encode all your data in folders, bypassing the "material realm" of files entirely and giving you infinite disk space (attempt at your own risk). Folders lang for code, Folders FS for data storage.
Visualizations
A Folders program is a nil-terminated nested list. Its simplest form is pure containment and order, like this all-array JSON:
That is also how the JS emulator saves/reads Folders programs.
However, other systems of visualization are possible. Folders programs are content as structure and can be applied to raw data of any type. Here is a Truth Machine as a contour map. The thicker lines are containers, and the order of folders is read starting at the upper left (NW corner) and proceeding counter-clockwise.
Other visualizations might be a family tree (with all single parents), a botanical branching structure (like a splitting stalk of wheat), or the paths through a maze.
The red dots indicate a threshhold from a container to a single child.
Language Spec
The language itself is a very simple imperative language with a short list of semantic rules.
For Commands and Expressions, the number of folders in their first child folder determines their use. Types are used directly.
Commands
| Command | # of Folders | Details | 
|---|---|---|
| if | 0 folders | Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands | 
| while | 1 folder | Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands | 
| declare | 2 folders | Second sub-folder holds type, third holds var name (in number of folders) | 
| let | 3 folders | Second holds var name (in number of folders), third holds expression | 
|  | 4 folders | Second sub-folder holds expression | 
| input | 5 folders | Second sub-folder holds var name | 
Expressions
| Type | # of Folders | Details | 
|---|---|---|
| variable | 0 folders | Second sub-folder holds var name | 
| add | 1 folder | Second sub-folder holds first expression to add, third holds second expression | 
| subtract | 2 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to subtract, third holds second expression | 
| multiply | 3 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to multiply, third holds second expression | 
| divide | 4 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to divide, third holds second expression | 
| literal value | 5 folders | Second sub-folder holds the type of the value (e.g. two folders for a string, third holds the value) | 
| equal to | 6 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
| greater than | 7 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
| less than | 8 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
Types
| Type | # of Folders | 
|---|---|
| float | 1 folder | 
| string | 2 folders | 
| char | 3 folders |

summary_raw: An agentic skills framework & software development methodology that works. [语言: Shell] [今日 +973 stars]
fulltext:
Superpowers is a complete software development methodology for your coding agents, built on top of a set of composable skills and some initial instructions that make sure your agent uses them.
It starts from the moment you fire up your coding agent. As soon as it sees that you're building something, it doesn't just jump into trying to write code. Instead, it steps back and asks you what you're really trying to do.
Once it's teased a spec out of the conversation, it shows it to you in chunks short enough to actually read and digest.
After you've signed off on the design, your agent puts together an implementation plan that's clear enough for an enthusiastic junior engineer with poor taste, no judgement, no project context, and an aversion to testing to follow. It emphasizes true red/green TDD, YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It), and DRY.
Next up, once you say "go", it launches a subagent-driven-development process, having agents work through each engineering task, inspecting and reviewing their work, and continuing forward. It's not uncommon for your agent to work autonomously for a couple hours at a time without deviating from the plan you put together.
There's a bunch more to it, but that's the core of the system. And because the skills trigger automatically, you don't need to do anything special. Your coding agent just has Superpowers.
If you're using Superpowers in enterprise and could benefit from commercial support, additional tooling, or managed spending, please don't hesitate to drop us a line at sales@primeradiant.com.
Installation differs by harness. If you use more than one, install Superpowers separately for each one.
Superpowers is available via the official Claude plugin marketplace
- Install the plugin from Anthropic's official marketplace: /plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official
The Superpowers marketplace provides Superpowers and some other related plugins for Claude Code.
- Register the marketplace: /plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace
- Install the plugin from this marketplace: /plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace
Install Superpowers as a plugin from this repository:
agy plugin install https://github.com/obra/superpowers
Antigravity lists each installed skill's description, and the description of
the using-superpowers skill prompts the model to load that skill at the start
of a conversation. Reinstall with the same command to update.
Superpowers is available via the official Codex plugin marketplace.
- In the Codex app, click on Plugins in the sidebar.
- You should see Superpowers in the Coding section.
- Click the + next to Superpowers and follow the prompts.
Superpowers is available via the official Codex plugin marketplace.
- Open the plugin search interface: /plugins
- Search for Superpowers: superpowers
- Select Install Plugin.
- In Cursor Agent chat, install from marketplace: /add-plugin superpowers
- Or search for "superpowers" in the plugin marketplace.
- Install the plugin from this repository: devin plugins install obra/superpowers
- Update to the latest version with: devin plugins update superpowers
- Register the marketplace: droid plugin marketplace add https://github.com/obra/superpowers
- Install the plugin: droid plugin install superpowers@superpowers
- Install the extension: gemini extensions install https://github.com/obra/superpowers
- Update later: gemini extensions update superpowers
- Register the marketplace: copilot plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace
- Install the plugin: copilot plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace
Superpowers is available via the official Grok plugin marketplace.
- Install the plugin from xAI's official marketplace: grok plugin install superpowers@xai-official --trust
- Or open the marketplace in the TUI, search for Superpowers, and install it: /marketplace
Superpowers is available in Kimi Code's plugin marketplace.
- Open Kimi Code's plugin manager: /plugins
- Go to Marketplace > Superpowers and install it.
- Or install directly from this repository: /plugins install https://github.com/obra/superpowers
- Detailed docs: docs/README.kimi.md
OpenCode uses its own plugin install; install Superpowers separately even if you already use it in another harness.
- Tell OpenCode: Fetch and follow instructions from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/obra/superpowers/refs/heads/main/.opencode/INSTALL.md
- Detailed docs: docs/README.opencode.md
Install Superpowers as a Pi package from this repository:
pi install git:github.com/obra/superpowers
For local development, run Pi with this checkout loaded as a temporary package:
pi -e /path/to/superpowers
The Pi package loads the Superpowers skills and a small extension that injects the using-superpowers bootstrap at session startup and again after compaction. Pi has native skills, so no compatibility Skill tool is required. Subagent and task-list tools remain optional Pi companion packages.
Qwen Code installs plugins from Claude Code marketplaces directly.
- Install the plugin from this repository, and pick superpowers when prompted:
qwen extensions install obra/superpowers
- Update later: qwen extensions update superpowers
Install Superpowers as a Hermes plugin from this repository:
hermes plugins install obra/superpowers --enable
Restart any active Hermes sessions after installing. Note: Hermes has no post-compaction hook, so a very long session that compacts over its first turn loses the bootstrap — start a fresh session if skills stop triggering.
Superpowers is available as a native Muse plugin — same repo, same skills, all harnesses. The using-superpowers bootstrap is injected via the native SessionStart hook alongside Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the rest — no per-session opt-in.
- Install from a local checkout: muse plugins install ./ muse plugins approve superpowers Or clone and install: git clone https://github.com/obra/superpowers.git muse plugins install ./superpowers muse plugins approve superpowers

[美剧] 幻视任务
我真的是幻视吗？
@潘誉晗：隐居在爱丁堡的幻视，平日里在一家酒吧打工，下班后，他会回到自己的思维意识里。那里有贾维斯、星期五、伊迪丝，托尼车库里的那对机械手臂 D.U.M-E 和 U ，甚至还有奥创。他满足这样的生活，每天循环。直到这天，他被赏金猎人追杀，女老板死了，然后他被告知，他的儿子汤米也被抓了。
上来就在虚拟空间里展示了来自史塔克工业所有 AI 的《幻视任务》，经费充足，紧接着就开启本次剧集的最大课题——白幻视对自我的追问。诞生于《旺达幻视》结局的他，拥有初代幻视的所有记忆。虽知晓了过往，但毕竟是没有亲身经历并感知过的事，所以一切对于他而言，陌生又熟悉——他是幻视，他又似乎不是幻视。起初他并不在乎这点，就当欣赏一部已知结局的电影，那个本以为只是魔法造物的儿子的出现，逼他不得不正视自己是谁的问题。
作为「旺达幻视」系列的终章，剧集探讨了爱与身份认同，真诚又深刻。
[美剧] 伊甸园之东
真是一个讨厌又迷人的蛇蝎美人。
@潘誉晗：是夜，一个女子挣扎着在地上匍匐前进，敲响了特拉斯克兄弟俩的家门。她伤痕累累，头上满是鲜血。在哥哥亚当的坚持下，他们收留了这名女子。自称凯茜的女子在亚当的悉心照顾下渐渐恢复。美丽的她看起来是那样动人，但弟弟查尔斯却觉得她不对劲。随后，亚当向凯茜求婚，并提出带她去加州展开新的生活。只是沉浸在喜悦中的亚当从未想过，这个决定会给家族带来致命的打击。
根据约翰·斯坦贝克同名小说所改编的剧集，围绕着美国文学历史上一位著名的恶女展开。女主角凯茜拥有一双能看透人的眼睛，可她并没有把这份聪慧用在正途上。她像是没有情感般，所有人都是她成功上位的工具，就连双亲、丈夫和儿子都能毫不留情地抛弃。细腻的镜头语言极其克制，却蕴含了浓厚的情感爆发，通过演员们的精湛演技，我们看到了人性的复杂，也看到了两代兄弟间，宛如该隐与亚伯的宿命悲剧。
[韩剧] 百日谎言
乱世里，一个扒手，又能做什么呢？
@潘誉晗：1932 年的京城府（即汉城），正值日军高压统治时期。贫民窟的少女李佳景是位天才扒手，复杂的成长背景，加上年幼时曾在美国传教士家做工的经历，使她精通日语和英语。一次偷盗，让她认识了伪装成外籍记者夫妇的爱国人士柳素兰与俞必立，还有被日本总督府二号人物收养的朝鲜孤儿佐藤英雄。被俞必立看中了天赋的李佳景，伪装成朝鲜总督府的翻译官，与学成归来同样担任翻译官的佐藤英雄，展开了一段浪漫又惊心动魄的爱情故事。
作为 tvN 二十周年的特别企划，剧集首播当天就拿下了一个好成绩。围绕着窃取日军机密密探与日军养子所展开的恋曲，有着那个时代下难以说清的愁绪。是正适合谈情说爱的年纪，也是两颗孤独灵魂的相遇，却因为国仇家恨，说不清也道不明。毕竟在那个自身难保的危险年代，个人的情爱只是小事，恋爱、真心、信任只是过眼烟云，为祖国的爱与奉献才是第一要义。
[日剧] 政盗鲁邦
窃钩者诛，窃国者侯。
@SHY：从不失手的怪盗如月弥生，潇洒半生却敌不过经济下行，陷入国民钱包空空而没钱可偷的境地。从电视新闻得到灵感的她，盯上了执政党国自党的秘密金库，誓要把黑金一扫而空。为了达成目标，弥生使出毕生所学，将游手好闲的政治家千金小早川雅推向政坛。
《非自然死亡》8 年后，编剧野木亚纪子和主演石原里美再度聚首，带来了一部设定吸睛的另类爽剧。一向喜欢针砭时弊的野木，在合适的舞台大显身手，且看弥生巧施连环计，让声名狼藉的政治素人一步步登上权力中心。石原的演技和气质依旧出挑，诠释怪盗捉摸不定的魅力，不止剧中的财物，仿佛还能偷走观众的心。
普通小偷提心吊胆能量微小，税金小偷合法敛财能量巨大，本作第 1 集「想偷钱，就去当国会议员」的台词，可谓正中靶心。虽然名义上是架空国家，剧中的设定几乎毫不掩饰，矛头直指日本的社会现状。围绕见不得光的政治黑金大做文章，改变积弊已久的制度僵局，这部兼具娱乐性和讽刺意味的剧集，后续展开值得期待。
[日剧] 豆与麦
- 关键词：剧情 / 美食 / 成长
- 又名：まめとむぎ
- 片长：30 分钟左右（单集；具体集数未知）；豆瓣链接
把腐烂变成发酵，是盐麹的魔法，也是人的魔法！
@利兹与青鸟：30 岁的时尚杂志编辑清水麦，因为个人能力太过突出而习惯单打独斗，没能升任总编辑。就像肥皂剧的开场，在事业失意之际，又被当场戳破是插足别人婚姻的第三者，受尽搓磨与白眼最终离职，职业梦想就这样惨淡收场。生活一团糟的小麦在一天晚上踏入了一间名为大豆堂的居酒屋，虽然店面被米田麻美继承，装潢和味道都焕然一新，但二人还是相谈甚欢、结下友谊，决定各取所长，共同经营店铺。
本剧改编自同名漫画，漫画作者是以《那你来做做看啊》闻名的谷口菜津子，本作也是一个以美食为核心、描绘成长与再生的疗愈故事。一个是清雅丽质努力认真的斋藤飞鸟，一个是开朗活泼圆嘟嘟的富田望生，两人凑在一起本就是双倍可爱；再加上日剧独特而细致的布景，无论是多灰败的心情，在大豆堂无数可爱玩偶和温暖灯光包围下，也会不知不觉变得雀跃起来；再听着咬下炸鸡块的脆响，看着热气氤氲的茶泡饭和慢慢露出惊喜神情的小麦，便能让人感叹「美食能治愈人心」果然不是一句虚言。
[英剧] 找春天
- 关键词：剧情 / 喜剧
- 又名：Youth
- 片长：28 分钟左右（单集）× 8 集；豆瓣链接
中年版《伦敦生活》。
@潘誉晗：亚历克斯是一名文学经纪人，身为单身母亲的她把儿子鲁阿里抚养成人。现在，鲁阿里终于要上大学了，她打算开始崭新的生活，因为这天她突然意识到，已 50 岁的她不再年轻。她认定女性到了 60 岁无法性感，决定抓住这最后十年，拥抱新的恋情。只是她没想到，才上大学的鲁阿里退学回了家，父亲的病情也开始恶化。
作为莎朗·豪根「自传三部曲」的收官之作，真实而深刻的剧集，成功记录了一位女性迟来的青春期。夹在上有老下有中间的亚历克斯，就连崩溃也要挑时间。作为一名女儿和母亲，她被不顺遂的生活拉扯着，无法喘口气。可亚历克斯，又真的做好重新开始的准备了吗？荣格说「如果你的潜意识没有进入你的意识，那就是你的命运」，所以在没有真正意识到应该首先爱自己之前，亚历克斯自以为的做好准备，其实也只是自欺欺人而已。因为 50 岁的人生并不可悲，只要你想，依然可以性感。
[澳大利亚] 尘落
被害者比加害者更重要。
@潘誉晗：刚 18 岁的少女伊迪，被人发现浑身赤裸地倒在甘蔗地里。接到报警后，刚调来的女警长蒂格忙赶到现场。调查中蒂格得知，本地在七个月前就发生过一起德国游客被下药并性侵的案件，只是最后案子不了了之。伊迪不记得任何事，最后的记忆停在前一晚的酒吧，而其中一名嫌疑人死了。
这部根据小说改编的小镇女警探案剧，早在今年 3 月就摘得 Séries Mania（法国系列剧狂欢节）的国际竞赛观众奖。发生在黄金海岸的故事，有着很正统的 Tropic Noir（热带黑色） 味，藏在阳光、沙滩这些元素下的黑暗，让人窒息。比起寻找真凶，剧集用更多的笔墨刻画了被害者的处境。伊迪明明婉拒了朋友更进一步的交往请求，也拒绝了粗鲁的男人，却不被相信，更要一遍遍努力地去回想不太记得的痛苦回忆，告诉自己要振作起来，但伤害已经造成，且成为了她身体的一部分。
其实比起找出真相，帮助被害者走出来更重要。
[美剧] 库比蒂诺
失业阵线联盟。
@潘誉晗：由《傲骨贤妻》团队打造的剧集《库比蒂诺》，这次把法庭战场搬到了硅谷，讲述了两个被公司开除的人，在为自己讨回公道后，决定开家小型律师事务所，专攻硅谷相关的案件，替那些被资本打压的牛马打工者维权。
罗伯特与米歇尔这对夫妻档确实值得相信，完美融合了律政与科技相关热点的剧集，节奏紧凑，又爽又能代入情绪。首集两位主人公的塑造就非常成功，我们看到了迈克尔希望挣脱父亲的枷锁，也明白奥利维亚渴望逃离保守的父母。他们被困在自己的人生课题里，因而变得现实。起初觉得只要维系了体面的工作，就是世俗意义上的成功，但这场被动的离职让两人看清了周遭的一切，也看清楚了现实——原来单纯的物质是无法给内心提供真正的丰盈。所以他们选择替硅谷的打工者们发声，不仅仅是为了开始一项新的事业，更为告诉那些为了大公司奉献了无数的牛马们，这个世界还有正义。
[美剧] 乔治和曼迪的头婚生活 第三季
不要在婚姻中撒谎。
@潘誉晗：因不满母亲玛丽可能开始的恋情，乔治禁止女儿与其见面。曼迪不认同这个决定，偷带着女儿去见玛丽；康纳因吸毒被警方逮捕，他不敢让父母和姐姐知道，转而向姐夫乔治求助，希望他能替自己递交保释金——乔治与曼迪这次都向彼此撒了谎。
高分情景喜剧《乔治和曼迪的头婚生活》第三季，依然围绕着乔治和曼迪的婚姻生活展开。在母剧中，我们提前知道了二人的结局，因而在这份上帝视角下看这段婚姻的发展，就很有趣。脱离了母剧里的四个天才，乔治与曼迪这对年轻工薪阶级夫妻的生活，普通而平凡。他们不需要去纠结深奥的物理问题，只需每天好好经营轮胎店的生意，注意平衡家庭生活，津津乐道地在乎着家里人的饮食起居，接地气到就像是生活中的你我他一样。但藏在寻常家庭生活里那些鸡毛蒜皮的小事，却是股积蓄力量的暗流，能慢慢影响这个家庭，然后提醒我们婚姻里的残酷与真实。
[动画] FX 战士久留美
老实赚钱，很枯燥吧？
@SHY：初中时，少女福贺久留美目睹母亲投资失败而跳楼自杀。那一刻，她下定决心，今后一定要赢下所有。5 年后，过了仅退款年龄的大学生久留美，终于能合法进行 FX 外汇交易。目标是用 30 万本金赚回母亲赔光的 2000 万日元，开弓没有回头箭的金钱游戏就此开始。
刚送走上季度的「尼古喵喵」，这边「拟股喵喵」便闪亮登场。顶着人畜无害的软萌画风，本作 4 位美少女主角的压迫感，远比一般恐怖片更可怕。由于货币汇率较为稳定，要从中获利，便需要数倍杠杆。然而，保证金终归有限，一点点技术性调整，就可能被强制平仓。真正意义上的生死一线，造就不寒而栗的现实梦魇。
知行合一的漫画原作者，内容取材亲身经历，更在社媒实时更新套牢动态。译者和读者同样不甘示弱，戏里戏外不分家的评论区众生相，带来独一份的沉浸式追更体验。深入刻画赌徒心理，梭哈只在一念之间，这则随折线起伏的非典型故事，是别人恐惧我贪婪的投资宝典，还是以史为鉴长心眼的劝退指南，相信诸位自有判断。
[动画] 学生会也有洞！
- 关键词：漫画改 / 日常 / 喜剧
- 又名：生徒会にも穴はある！ / Even the Student Council Has Its Holes!
- 片长：24 分钟（单集）× 12 集，每周六更新
- 观看渠道：巴哈姆特动画疯；豆瓣链接
神人越多，神人越神！
@SHY：文思泉涌的高一学生水之江梅，文科成绩遥遥领先，理科成绩惨不忍睹，平均分到了要留级的地步。为了避免危机，在顾问平冢老师的推荐下，成为学生会书记的他，却发现其他成员个个不是省油的灯。被一帮奇葩成员重重包围，阿梅五彩缤纷的校园生活揭开序幕。
《妄想学生会》完结不久，一部精神续作便在同杂志横空出世，风格颇具前辈神韵，黄暴程度有增无减。以鲜明的角色属性为卖点，纯情闷骚的会长古都吹寿子、文静腹黑的会计照井有栖、毒舌嚣张的宣传委员尾鸟绽，以及只是在努力活着的庶务陆奥驹絽，共同编织节操全无的欢脱日常，一脚踩断刹车，整活绝不能停。
导演龙轮直征 × 人设今村亮的金牌组合，尽兴挥洒夸张的演出效果，以简约线条营造极致动感，打造同样个性十足的动画体验。巧妙整合本是四格的原著段子，把握名场面层出不穷的快节奏叙事，任何时候点开都不会无聊。主打活泼奔放的喧闹日常，不忘加以浪漫和温馨点缀，这出骚动时节的青春喜剧，定能挑逗你的心。
[动画] 某暗部的少女共栖
再也没有这样的好姐妹了！
@SHY：人口约八成都是学生的巨大「学园都市」，拥有远超外界的科技水平，更实施着开发超能力的特殊课程。而在梦幻般的和平表象之下，却有着不存于世的暗部，这是 Level 5 超能力者麦野沈利领导的精锐部队「道具」，及其成员绢旗最爱、芙兰达·塞维伦、泷壶理后的故事。
「超炮 T」完结 6 年后，「某系列」动画终于上新，改编自镰池和马创作的外传小说，本作的时间线约在本篇 1 年前，进一步补完了「道具」的角色塑造，相信也能让观众产生稍有不同的印象。不忘初心的系列导演长井龙雪，回归舒适区后状态绝佳，完全原创的动画第 1 集编排合理，也让那几位熟悉的角色顺势露面。
近些年饱受诟病的 J.C.STAFF，对本系列从来不敢懈怠，作画质量维持在水准线上。好久不见的学园超能力战斗，现在看来依然颇有可取之处，即使已经知道部分角色的结局，也不妨碍欣赏当下的少女羁绊。这则糅合了各种元素的故事，无缝衔接日常与非日常，是系列粉丝不容错过的外传，也是新观众可以独立观看的全新冒险。
[动画] 闹鬼酒店 第二季
是时候重返这家诡异的酒店了。
@潘誉晗：凯瑟琳计划招募一位新员工，也正是在这时，他他们惊讶地发现一位名叫 Shayna 的女生，原来不是鬼魂，而是活生生的人类。这一年来，她一直寄住在阁楼里。请她离开后，凯瑟琳录用了一位和自己同名的员工，这位员工有着很丰富的酒店工作经验，只是不知为何，这位新员工就像是猫薄荷般的存在，酒店里的所有生物都对其非常痴迷。
《闹鬼酒店》的第二季依然围绕着酒店展开，本以为酒店的生意终于进入了正轨，谁料却冒出了更多的新麻烦。神秘的紫色黏液只要一触碰就会失去理智，酒店下的旧矿井拥有受诅咒的矿石……只是经营好酒店可能还容易一些，阻止超自然世界生物所造成的各种麻烦，才是凯瑟琳一行人优先需要关注的事。
